conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m glad we have this time together.  
I’d like to do a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—better known as the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-item questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. Anything you share stays strictly between us unless there’s an urgent safety concern, and my only goal is to support you. We’ll move through the questions at your pace; they’re about the past seven days. Ready to start?

1. In the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly… not very often. I can maybe force a little laugh if someone else is joking, but it doesn’t feel natural—like I’m just pretending. Most of the time the best I manage is a half-smile, and even that feels like work.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I can’t remember the last time I actually laughed. Even when my partner tries to joke with me, it just feels flat. I’ll maybe give a polite smile, but inside I still feel heavy, like nothing is really funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes… I still get a tiny spark of excitement about little things—like my favorite TV show coming on—but it fades fast. Mostly I just feel kind of numb or like “what’s the point?” I used to really look forward to coffee with friends or a walk, but now it feels like I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not a good enough mom. Even when my partner says it’s normal, I still replay everything in my head and find ways it must be my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not breathing right, or I’ll lie awake imagining her crib tipping over or the stroller rolling into the street. I know the chances are tiny, but I can’t switch the thoughts off; they just loop until I’m exhausted.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes... a few times this week. Out of nowhere my chest gets tight and I feel like I can't breathe. Once I was just folding laundry and suddenly I was sure something awful was about to happen to the baby. It passes after a few minutes, but in that moment it feels like I'm going to die.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. I’ll start the morning thinking “I just have to get through feeds and laundry,” but by noon it feels like I’m drowning—dishes pile up, the baby won’t nap, and I’m running on three broken hours of sleep. I keep telling myself “push through,” but it’s like I’m stuck in wet cement; every little chore feels ten times heavier.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes... I dread bedtime. As soon as the house is quiet, my mind starts racing with all the "what-ifs" about the baby. I lie there for an hour or more, and when I do fall asleep I wake up every couple of hours with my heart pounding. Even when she's sleeping soundly, I can't seem to settle.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I feel sad more days than not. It’s like this gray cloud that just hangs over everything. I’ll be feeding her and tears start rolling down my face and I can’t even explain why. I keep thinking I should feel grateful, but instead I just feel empty and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

That’s me, most days. I’ll be changing her diaper and suddenly I’m crying. Or when my mom calls to check in, I can’t get through the conversation without tearing up. It’s like the tears are right there all the time—I just try to hide them so nobody worries.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…a couple of times this week, yeah. Nothing planned—just these quick flashes like “what if I weren’t here?” when everything feels too heavy. I always push the thought away right after, because I’d never leave my baby, but it still scares me that it pops in at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 29: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]  
Clinician: [licensed provider]

Patient-reported findings (10-item EPDS-style interview):

1. Anhedonia: marked reduction in ability to laugh or experience pleasure; even previously enjoyable activities feel “flat” or pointless.  
2. Persistent low mood: daily feelings of emptiness, tearfulness, “gray cloud”; spontaneous crying spells.  
3. Subjective guilt / self-blame: recurrent, excessive self-criticism regarding infant care (“not a good enough mom”).  
4. Anxious preoccupation: near-daily intrusive worries about infant safety, racing heart, difficulty dismissing catastrophic thoughts.  
5. Panic symptoms: multiple episodes this week of sudden chest tightness, breathlessness, dread “something awful” will happen.  
6. Overwhelm / impaired coping: describes “drowning,” tasks feeling “ten times heavier,” stuck in “wet cement.”  
7. Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia and middle-night wakening linked to racing anxious thoughts, independent of infant sleep.  
8. Frequency of crying: majority of days, often unprovoked.  
9. Self-harm ideation: fleeting passive thoughts “what if I weren’t here?” twice this week; no plan or intent reported; patient immediately dismisses and expresses protective feelings toward infant.

Screening significance:  
• Meets probable cut-off for major depressive and anxiety symptoms postpartum.  
• Safety concern: presence of any self-harm thought, however fleeting, warrants further risk assessment.

Next steps:  
• Recommend full diagnostic evaluation (DSM-5-TR criteria) and safety plan today.  
• Consider referral for perinatal-trained mental health provider and/or mother-infant psychiatric service.  
• Provide emergency resources (24/7 hotline, local ED) and instructions to return immediately if thoughts escalate or intent develops.

End of screening note
